C004.subject: Higher protein intake (≥2.4 g/kg body weight) in a 16:8 time-restricted feeding protocol
C004.object: 24-hour energy expenditure beyond the thermic effect of food alone during an energy deficit exceeding 25%
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Higher protein intake (≥2.4 g/kg body weight) in a 16:8 time-restricted feeding protocol 24-hour energy expenditure beyond the thermic effect of food alone during an energy deficit exceeding 25%]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled metabolic chamber study comparing 24-hour energy expenditure in participants on a 16:8 time-restricted feeding protocol with high protein (≥2.4 g/kg) vs. normal protein intake during a >25% energy deficit — Direct measurement of total daily energy expenditure via whole-room calorimetry would isolate effects beyond the thermic effect of food, testing whether high protein under these specific conditions elevates EE through non-TEF mechanisms.

[PATH:empirical] Muscle biopsy analysis for markers of mitochondrial uncoupling (e.g., UCP1, UCP3 expression, proton leak) in human subjects after 2+ weeks of the described diet and feeding schedule — The proposed mechanism involves enhanced mitochondrial uncoupling in skeletal muscle; measuring these molecular markers in muscle tissue provides a direct test of the hypothesized pathway.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review of existing literature on protein intake, time-restricted feeding, and energy expenditure during severe energy deficits, with meta-analysis of studies measuring 24h EE via doubly labeled water or calorimetry — A comprehensive synthesis of available data can assess whether the effect is consistently observed across studies, identify effect size, and evaluate the strength of evidence for the proposed mechanism.

qualifier.mechanism: enhanced mitochondrial uncoupling in skeletal muscle

C005.subject: Higher protein intake (≥2.4 g/kg body weight) in a 16:8 time-restricted feeding protocol
C005.object: residual metabolic adaptation during an energy deficit exceeding 25%
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: Higher protein intake (≥2.4 g/kg body weight) in a 16:8 time-restricted feeding protocol residual metabolic adaptation during an energy deficit exceeding 25%]

[PATH:empirical] Controlled crossover trial comparing isocaloric 25% energy deficit with 16:8 TRF, varying protein intake (2.4 vs 1.6 g/kg) while measuring resting metabolic rate via indirect calorimetry at baseline and week 4. — Directly tests the hypothesis by isolating protein level as the independent variable and residual metabolic adaptation as the outcome, within the specified short-term TRF protocol and energy deficit threshold.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of time-restricted feeding studies with energy deficits >25%, stratified by protein intake (≥2.4 g/kg vs lower), using individual participant data to assess change in RMR adjusted for fat-free mass loss. — Synthesizes existing data across multiple studies to increase statistical power and detect whether protein intake modifies metabolic adaptation, addressing the disputed status with broader evidence.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic study measuring 24-h nitrogen balance, whole-body protein turnover (using stable isotope tracers), and mitochondrial efficiency in muscle biopsies during the intervention. — Tests the theoretical basis: whether high protein intake preserves lean mass and thermic effect of feeding enough to offset the adaptive thermogenesis expected from severe energy restriction, thus explaining the null effect.

C006.subject: Higher protein intake (≥2.4 g/kg body weight) in a 16:8 time-restricted feeding protocol

[PATH:empirical] Randomized crossover trial comparing 2.4 g/kg vs. 1.6 g/kg protein (animal-based) in a 16:8 TRF protocol with 25% energy deficit, measuring plasma ghrelin AUC and VAS hunger scores over 4 weeks — Directly tests the hypothesis under specified conditions (animal-based protein, short-term) with appetite biomarkers and subjective ratings, providing causal evidence for attenuation.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of high-protein diets (>2.0 g/kg) on ghrelin suppression during energy restriction, stratified by protein source (animal vs. plant) and feeding timing (TRF vs. continuous) — Synthesizes existing data to assess whether the effect is robust across studies and whether the animal-based qualifier is a necessary condition, clarifying generalizability and potential mechanisms.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic study in rodents or humans examining the effect of animal-based protein (e.g., whey vs. soy) on ghrelin O-acyltransferase (GOAT) activity and vagal afferent signaling under time-restricted feeding — Tests the biological plausibility that animal protein specifically modulates ghrelin acylation or gut-brain signaling, which could explain the attenuated hunger response and identify confounders.

qualifier.condition: if the protein source is predominantly animal-based

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing 16:8 time-restricted feeding with high protein (≥2.4 g/kg) vs. standard protein (1.2-1.6 g/kg) over 12 weeks in a >25% energy deficit, measuring resting metabolic rate via indirect calorimetry and dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry for body composition — Directly tests the hypothesis under controlled conditions, isolating the effect of protein level on metabolic adaptation during the specified temporal scope and energy deficit.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of protein intake levels and metabolic adaptation in energy-restricted diets, with subgroup analysis on intermittent fasting protocols including time-restricted feeding — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether higher protein consistently attenuates metabolic slowing across studies, addressing the disputed status and providing statistical power to confirm or refute the claim.

[PATH:empirical] Mechanistic study examining the effect of high protein (≥2.4 g/kg) on thermic effect of food, muscle protein synthesis, and mitochondrial efficiency during 16:8 time-restricted feeding in a controlled metabolic ward — Investigates underlying physiological mechanisms (e.g., increased diet-induced thermogenesis, preservation of lean mass) that could explain mitigated metabolic adaptation, providing causal evidence to support or contradict the hypothesis.

qualifier.temporal: during the first 12 weeks of intervention
